steps.tx: An **acute haematogenous osteomyelitis** is a serious bacterial bone infection predominantly affecting growing children, with peak incidence between three and twelve years of age. Staphylococcus aureus causes more than eighty percent of cases worldwide. In neonates, Group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli are frequent, whereas Salmonella species assume paramount clinical importance in children with sickle cell haemoglobinopathy.
steps.say: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis is a severe bone infection primarily affecting children between three and twelve years. Staphylococcus aureus causes over eighty percent of all cases. In newborns, think of group B strep and E. coli, while in patients with sickle cell disease, Salmonella is classic.

steps.tx: Look closely at the lower femoral metaphysis on this film. An area of bone has been destroyed, and inside the cavity sits a dense dead fragment separated from living bone, while new bone thickens around the outside. That dead fragment is the **sequestrum**, and its presence tells you infection has progressed beyond a simple early metaphyseal focus.
steps.say: On this femoral film destroyed metaphysis contains a dense dead fragment, the sequestrum, wrapped by new outer bone. Its presence shows osteomyelitis has advanced beyond an early focus.

steps.tx: The distinctive predilection for the **metaphyseal vascular loops** reflects unique pediatric vascular anatomy. Nutrient arterioles terminate in sluggish, non-anastomosing venous sinusoidal loops adjacent to the epiphyseal growth plate. These loops lack functional phagocytic reticuloendothelial lining, creating a micro-environment where transient bacteremia readily seeds, triggering thrombosis, purulent exudation, and rapid intra-medullary pressure escalation.
steps.say: The infection targets the metaphysis because of its unique blood supply. Terminal nutrient arteries make sharp hairpin loops into slow-flowing venous lakes right beneath the growth plate. These loops lack active phagocytic cells, allowing circulating bacteria to settle, multiply, and spark thrombosis and pus formation.

left.title: Metaphyseal Predisposition
points: Hairpin loops with turbulent, sluggish flow
High metabolic turnover in rapid growth

right.title: Epiphyseal Protection
points: Physeal cartilage acts as an avascular barrier
Prevents direct intra-articular spread in older children
Except in transphyseal vessels of infants under 1 year

steps.tx: As pus accumulates, it tracks through cortical Haversian and Volkmann canals to strip the loose pediatric periosteum, compromising cortical blood flow. The devascularized, necrotic bone segment that detaches is designated a **sequestrum**. Concurrently, the elevated, living periosteum deposits reactive new subperiosteal bone termed the involucrum, which encloses the necrotic core, while cloacae form discharging sinuses.
steps.say: As pus builds up under pressure, it burrows through tiny cortical channels and peels the periosteum off the bone. Deprived of blood, a segment of dead bone separates as a sequestrum. Meanwhile, the stripped periosteum lays down a rigid sleeve of new living bone called the involucrum, punctured by cloacae that vent pus to the skin.

vis.title: Pathological Hallmarks of Osteomyelitis
rows: Dense, sclerotic, chalky white fragment with clear halo
Irregular thickened bony sleeve enclosing sequestrum

steps.tx: Clinical diagnosis hinges on point bone tenderness, refusal to bear weight, and high spiking fever. Initial plain radiographs remain completely normal for the first seven to ten days, displaying only subtle deep soft tissue swelling. **Magnetic resonance imaging** represents the definitive early diagnostic modality, revealing intense bone marrow oedema and subperiosteal fluid collections within twenty-four hours of symptom onset.
steps.say: Always suspect osteomyelitis in a child with high fever and severe, pinpoint bone tenderness who refuses to walk. Plain X-rays look completely normal for the first week to ten days, showing only faint muscle swelling. Magnetic resonance imaging is the investigation of choice, lighting up marrow edema and subperiosteal pus within hours.

left.title: Early Stage (Days 1 to 7)
points: Blood cultures positive in 40 to 50 percent
MRI detects marrow oedema within 24 hours

steps.tx: Immediate management demands blood cultures followed by targeted intravenous bactericidal antibiotics. Urgent surgical intervention via **cortical drilling** or fenestration is indicated whenever a subperiosteal abscess is identified on ultrasound, or when toxic systemic signs and localized tenderness fail to improve after twenty-four to forty-eight hours of appropriate intravenous antimicrobial therapy, venting the medullary canal.
steps.say: Draw blood cultures and start high dose intravenous antibiotics immediately. If ultrasound or MRI shows a subperiosteal abscess, or if fever and severe pain persist after twenty-four to forty-eight hours of antibiotics, operate without delay. Drill holes in the cortex to vent the marrow cavity and relieve hydrostatic pressure.

vis.title: Indications for Surgical Decompression
rows: Persistent fever, rising CRP, severe pain
Evacuates medullary pus; salvages blood supply

quiz.q: Why is the metaphysis of rapidly growing pediatric long bones preferentially seeded in haematogenous osteomyelitis?
options: Sluggish blood flow in terminal hairpin sinusoidal loops lacking phagocytic cells
Absence of cortical bone allowing direct bacterial invasion from skin
Hypertrophied lymphatic drainage concentrating bacterial emboli
Direct communication with the epiphyseal vascular arcade across the physis
quiz.explain: The metaphysis possesses terminal arterial loops emptying into slow-flowing venous sinusoids that lack functional phagocytic reticuloendothelial cells, facilitating bacterial seeding during transient bacteraemia.

quiz.q: How long after the onset of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis do bony changes first become visible on plain radiographs?
quiz.explain: Plain radiographs remain entirely normal for the first 7 to 10 days; early findings are limited to soft tissue swelling until 30 to 50 percent of bone mineral is lost.
